ref: DAR — Revelation ch. 16: The Plagues Poured Out
title: The Plagues Poured Out
voicePrompt: In your own words, explain Smith's two-part thesis about the seven last plagues: why he argues their judgments are literal yet entirely future (after probation closes), and walk through how the chronology proof, the sixth plague on the Euphrates, and Armageddon support that case.

questions.stem: According to Smith, what proves the chronology of the plagues — that is, when they fall?
options: The first plague is poured on those who have the mark of the beast and worship his image, the very work the third angel warns against, so the plagues cannot fall until that angel closes his work
The plagues began in the days of ancient Egypt and run parallel to the Egyptian plagues
The plagues are scattered across all of church history, one per century
The seventh plague falls first, fixing the start at the second coming
questions.explanation: Smith argues the description of the first plague reveals its chronology: it falls on those with the mark of the beast and who worship his image, the identical work against which the third angel warns. This is 'conclusive proof' that the judgments are not poured out until after that angel closes his work.

questions.stem: How does the fifth plague serve as evidence that the plagues are NOT spread across centuries in the past?
options: Under the fifth plague men still suffer the sores caused by the first plague, showing all the plagues fall on one and the same generation
The fifth plague is explicitly dated to the fall of pagan Rome
The fifth plague describes events nobody could survive, so it must be symbolic
The fifth plague is poured on the sea, repeating the second plague
questions.explanation: Smith notes that under the fifth plague men blaspheme God because of their sores — the same sores caused by the first plague. Since the same people survive from the first plague to the fifth, the plagues must fall on one generation, which is 'utterly subversive' of the view that they began in the past and occupy centuries each.

questions.stem: What does Smith say Revelation 15:8 ('the temple was filled with smoke... no man was able to enter... till the seven plagues were fulfilled') establishes about the plagues?
options: That the plagues fall only on the literal city of Jerusalem
That there is no ministration in the heavenly sanctuary during the plagues, so they follow the close of Christ's mediation
That the plagues are symbolic visions seen only in the temple
That the seven angels are the same as the seven churches
questions.explanation: Smith identifies this temple as the heavenly sanctuary. Because no being can enter it until the plagues are fulfilled, there is no ministration in the sanctuary during this time; the vials are poured out only at the close of Christ's ministration above, when 'Christ is then no longer a mediator.'

questions.stem: Why does Smith insist the plagues' judgments are literal rather than merely symbolic?
options: Because John explicitly calls each vial a parable
Because the plagues are almost identical to those God literally inflicted on the Egyptians, whose literality is seldom questioned, as God again delivers his people
Because every symbol in Revelation is decoded in chapter 16 itself
Because the angels in the chapter say the plagues are figures of speech
questions.explanation: Smith sees 'no apparent reason' why the first plague should not be strictly literal, noting these plagues are almost identical to those God inflicted on the Egyptians when delivering His people — judgments whose literality is seldom questioned. As God crowns His people with final deliverance, His judgments will be no less literal and terrible.

questions.stem: How can the last generation of the wicked be said to have 'shed the blood of saints and prophets' if the final generation of saints is not slain?
options: They literally execute all the saints before the plagues begin
Guilt attaches to motive as well as action; they form the determined purpose to slaughter the saints, so in motive they are as guilty as if they had carried it out
The phrase refers only to literal prophets killed in Old Testament times
Smith says the verse is a copyist's error and should be ignored
questions.explanation: Citing Matthew 23 and 1 John 3:15, Smith argues guilt attaches to motive no less than to action. The present generation forms a determined purpose to devote the saints to indiscriminate slaughter, so 'in motive and purpose, they do shed the blood of saints and prophets, and are every whit as guilty' as if they had carried it out.

questions.stem: In Smith's interpretation, what does the 'great river Euphrates' of the sixth plague symbolize?
options: The literal river in Asia, which must be physically dried up for an army to cross
The Roman Catholic papacy seated at Rome
The Ottoman, or Turkish, empire that holds the territory watered by the river
The river of life flowing from the throne of God
questions.explanation: Smith rejects the literal-river view (drying a river would be no serious judgment, the Tigris is ignored, the rivers already dry up under the fourth plague) and reads the Euphrates figuratively as the power holding its territory — the Ottoman, or Turkish, empire. Its 'drying up' is the consumption of that empire, producing literal judgments on men.

questions.stem: How does Smith say the drying up of the Euphrates 'prepares the way of the kings of the east'?
options: By literally exposing a riverbed road for marching armies
By removing the Turkish power that holds Palestine and Jerusalem, opening the way for the nations to rally to the Holy Land for the final battle
By converting the Mohammedan nations to Christianity
By drying up the Mississippi, which he calls the true eastern river
questions.explanation: Smith explains the battle is to be fought near Jerusalem, which Turkey holds. When the European powers withdraw the support that has propped up the sultan to preserve the 'balance of power,' Turkey will be no more and 'the way will be all open for the nations to make their last grand rally to the Holy Land.'

questions.stem: Regarding 'he gathered them together... Armageddon' (verse 16), what conclusion does Smith reach?
options: Christ gathers the saints to the New Jerusalem for the marriage supper of the Lamb
The unclean spirits gather the wicked kings of the earth to the battle of the great day of God Almighty, so the gathered are Satan's minions, not saints
The angels gather the dead for the resurrection
The verse describes the saints fleeing to the mountains for safety
questions.explanation: Smith reviews the Greek (a neuter plural 'the spirits' taking a singular verb) and several translations rendering it 'they gathered.' He concludes the persons gathered are 'the minions of Satan, not saints,' that it is the work of the spirits, not of Christ, and that the place is Armageddon for 'the battle of that great day of God Almighty,' not the New Jerusalem.
